# Why the crowd on the right side of the frame is turned to their left

## Short answer

They are turned that way because that is the direction the President and the
podium are in. The people in the right half of the picture have rotated their
heads (and in many cases their whole upper bodies) away from the direction their
seats point, so that they can watch and listen to the man speaking at the
lectern. They are not looking at anything to the right of them; they are looking
*past* the camera position, toward the stage — which, from where they are
sitting, lies off to their left.

## What the picture shows

The photograph is of Barack Obama giving a speech in a large indoor arena. The
evidence for that reading is all in the frame: the lectern in front of him
carries the Seal of the President of the United States; two presidential-style
microphones are clamped to it; a teleprompter panel on a stand rises at the left
of the frame; and he is caught mid-sentence with his mouth open and his right
arm extended in a gesture. Overhead, a blue banner reads "...LTH CARE" (i.e.
"HEALTH CARE"), so this is a health-care speech or rally. Team banners and red
"MARYLAND" sweatshirts in the crowd, plus the tiered seating, railings,
vomitory portals and a raised basketball backboard high on the right, indicate a
college basketball arena packed for the event — most likely Obama's health-care
rally at the University of Maryland's Comcast Center in September 2009.

## Why the turn is to their left specifically

In an arena the seats are built to face the court, so the crowd is arranged in a
ring and different sections naturally point in different directions. Nobody's
seat is aimed at the lectern, because the lectern is not at the centre of the
floor — the stage for an event like this is set up at one side of the floor, and
the photographer is standing just in front of it, shooting back across the room.

That produces exactly the geometry in the image. The spectators visible behind
Obama are on the far side of the arena, so their seats point across the floor,
broadly toward the camera. The podium, however, is much nearer to the camera
than the centre of the floor is, and it sits off to one side of the line their
seats point along. For the sections on the right of the frame, that offset falls
on their left-hand side, so to put the speaker in front of their faces they have
to swivel leftward. The further right in the frame a person is, the larger that
angle is — which is why the faces near the right edge are seen almost in
profile, while those nearer the middle are close to full-face.

Note also that this same turn reads, from the viewer's side of the camera, as
their faces being angled toward the *left of the picture* — that is, toward the
President at the centre of the frame. Under either reading of "their left," the
cause is the same: the speaker is the focus, and he is off to that side.

## Supporting evidence inside the image

1. **The crowd converges on the lectern.** The people in the left half of the
   frame are turned the opposite way — angled slightly toward the right of the
   picture. The two halves point at each other, and the intersection of their
   sightlines falls on Obama at the centre. That is the signature of a single
   shared focus of attention rather than a general drift in one direction.
2. **The turn grows with distance from the centre.** Faces just right of Obama
   are nearly frontal; those out at the right-hand edge are strongly rotated.
   That gradient is what you get when a whole seating bowl is looking at one
   fixed point that is closer to the camera than they are.
3. **They are engaged with him, not distracted.** Many are applauding, some are
   standing, several are holding up phones and cameras — and those devices are
   aimed the same way the faces are pointed. On the left side of the frame a man
   is holding a camera up and aiming it toward the right, at Obama.
4. **There is nothing else to look at on the right.** The right-hand part of the
   frame contains only more seating, a stairway railing, a dark portal with a
   couple of staff standing in it, and a stowed basketball backboard. No second
   stage, no screen, no commotion.

## Alternatives that do not fit

- *Watching a video screen or scoreboard:* an arena's video board hangs high
  over the middle of the floor, so heads would be tilted noticeably upward and
  all converging on one high point. These heads are level or only slightly
  raised, and their sightlines converge low, at podium height.
- *Reacting to a disturbance, a late arrival or something happening off-frame:*
  that would show as a scatter of surprised or craning postures with people
  half-standing and looking in a common direction outside the picture. Instead
  the postures are relaxed and attentive, with clapping and filming — the body
  language of an audience watching a speaker.
- *Simply the way the seats are bolted down:* the seats in that part of the bowl
  point across the floor, not at the stage; these people are visibly rotated

The man at the podium is Barack Obama, photographed from the front as he speaks, with his right arm extended toward image-left.

The crowd visible behind him is therefore seated behind the stage. Those people see the back of Obama and the back of the podium, not his face.

In the right half of the image many of those spectators have their heads turned so that in the photograph they look toward image-right. Since they are themselves facing generally forward toward the arena floor and camera, image-right is toward their own left.

The most likely reason is that they are watching a large off-camera arena video screen, to their left-front and to image-right, showing a close-up of Obama as he speaks.

This explains three observations explicitly:

1. The direction is shared. Several neighboring people — for example the man in white, the boy in yellow, the person in the green cap, the woman in purple, and the man in the red cap in the stands just right of the podium — all face the same way, toward image-right, away from the real podium which lies to image-left of them.

2. The direction is away from the speaker himself. The podium is to image-left of these spectators. If they were looking directly at Obama they would have to turn toward their own right, not their left.

3. Cameras point the same way. A woman with a still camera and another spectator with a phone/camera in that section hold their cameras up and point them toward image-right, away from the real Obama. A person does not photograph the back of a speaker when the speaker's magnified front view is available; they photograph the screen.

At a large in-the-round health-care rally of this kind that behavior is normal: spectators stuck behind the speaker follow his face and expressions on a side Jumbotron/monitor rather than staring at his back.
